name: Chalkida
title: Chalkida Ship UTM: Thickness Gauging at Chalkis Shipyards
description: Ship thickness measurement in Chalkida for bulk carriers, tankers and ferries docking at Chalkis Shipyards or waiting off Evia: hull, hold and tank UTM.
h1: Hull Gauging and Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement in Chalkida, Evia
intro: Chalkida, on Evia's western coast where the Euripus narrows to its tightest point, combines a working shipyard with a cargo port and one of the most unusual passages in Greek waters. Bulk carriers, tankers, general cargo ships and ferries come to Chalkis Shipyards for docking, retrofits and repairs, while others wait in the gulf for the old bridge to open or for a cargo. Every one of those stops is a chance to gauge. Our technicians make the trip from India for each vessel and work wherever it lies.

highlights.h: A working drydock yard on Evia
highlights.p: Chalkis Shipyards docks merchant ships up to about Supramax size for surveys, repairs, ballast water system retrofits, hold treatment and conversions. The dock period is the moment to measure bottom, shell, holds and tanks, with renewal decided before the ship refloats and leaves the yard.

Ships passing between the north and south Euboean gulfs depend on the old bridge opening and on the strait's reversing currents. Waits on either side, often overnight, can be put to use for deck and tank readings by launch, arranged through the ship's agent.

Handysize and Supramax bulk carriers form much of the yard's work, many of them Greek-managed and approaching their later renewal surveys. Hold frames, hopper and topside tanks and hatch coamings are the areas where measured data most often changes the steel list.

port.h: Chalkida and the Euripus: narrows, shipyard and cargo port
p: Chalkida stands at the Euripus Strait, the narrow channel that separates the island of Evia from the Greek mainland and links the North and South Euboean Gulfs. At its narrowest point the strait is crossed by an old low bridge that opens to let ships through, and a high-level road bridge spans the water a little further south. The Euripus is famous for its tidal currents, which change direction several times a day and run hard through the gap, so passages are timed to the current and to the bridge opening rather than to the ship's convenience. Ships approaching from the south come up the South Euboean Gulf from the Aegean, while those from the north come down through the Oreoi channel and the North Euboean Gulf.

Shipping at Chalkida falls into three groups. The first is repair traffic: bulk carriers, tankers, general cargo ships, ferries and smaller vessels that come to the shipyard for drydocking, class surveys, retrofits and conversions, many of them managed from Piraeus and Athens, which are within easy driving distance. The second is cargo, as the port and private quays along the gulfs handle bulk materials and general cargo for industries in central Greece and on Evia itself. The third is passage traffic, mainly coasters and smaller cargo ships using the strait as a short cut between the ports of the North Euboean Gulf and the Aegean, which saves them the long passage around Evia's exposed eastern coast and the Kafireas channel.

Because the Euripus imposes its own timetable, ships here are often kept waiting, at anchor in the South Euboean Gulf below the high bridge or in the northern gulf above the old one, until a passage slot opens. Both gulfs are enclosed and generally sheltered, and the Mediterranean tide, so small elsewhere, matters here only through the currents it drives in the strait. Ferries and coastal ships tend to dock in winter, while deep-sea ships come through the year as their surveys fall due, and summer brings more yacht and leisure traffic through the narrows. For gauging, the practical windows are the dock period at the yard, lay-by time at its quays after undocking, and the waits on either side of the strait.

facilities.h: Gauging at Chalkis Shipyards and around the Euripus
p: Chalkis Shipyards is the centre of the work. The yard dry-docks merchant ships up to roughly Supramax size and handles ballast water treatment installations, cargo hold treatment, steel and piping repairs and conversions, with its own quays for afloat work before and after docking. It operates under the ISPS Code, so entry is by pass arranged in advance. The yard has also announced an investment in a larger, Panamax-size floating dock, which would widen the range of ships it can take. For gauging, the order of work matters most: readings in holds and tanks taken in the first days in dock give the yard and the attending surveyor time to agree renewal while staging is still rigged.

Outside the yard, the work is done afloat. Ships at anchor waiting for the strait or a berth are boarded by launch arranged through the agent, which suits deck, hatch cover and ballast tank gauging when the crew can prepare tanks in advance. Cargo ships working at the Chalkida quays or at private berths along the gulfs can be gauged during cargo operations, hold by hold as they are emptied. A ship heading for the yard can also be gauged at anchor beforehand, so it arrives with a steel estimate rather than a list of suspected areas, which is especially useful when the dock period is short and plate stock has to be confirmed before work starts.

context.h: Rules, retrofits and older tonnage at Chalkida
p: Chalkida is under the Paris MoU, with port state control and the regulation of passage through the Euripus in the hands of the Hellenic Coast Guard and the local harbour master. A ship under repair is still a foreign-flagged ship in an EU port, so PSC can attend one leaving the yard as easily as one arriving with cargo. Ships calling at EU ports need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, and that inventory has to be updated whenever a yard period adds or removes equipment, which makes it directly relevant to the conversions and retrofits carried out at Chalkida.

The retrofit work itself shapes gauging scopes. Ballast water treatment systems, scrubbers and other equipment fitted in recent years have brought new pipe runs, overboard penetrations and foundations into older hulls, and those areas corrode in their own way. When a ship docks at Chalkida for a renewal survey, owners often add these systems to the thickness measurement scope alongside the traditional hold and tank structure. Many of the bulk carriers seen at the yard are Handysize and Supramax ships of Greek ownership in their second decade, where the third or fourth renewal survey decides whether a ship keeps trading. Measured data on cargo holds, side shell frames and topside tanks lets the owner make that call on facts rather than estimates.

jobs.p: Most Chalkida jobs are linked to a docking. The superintendent sends the survey due, the yard dates and the class, and we plan the readings so the heaviest areas are measured first once the ship is in dock. Pre-docking work at anchor in the gulf comes next, followed by cargo-call gauging at the quays and the occasional condition survey on a ship waiting for the strait. Because the yard handles retrofits as well as surveys, scopes often combine hull structure with piping, including ballast water and scrubber lines installed in recent years. Results go to the superintendent and the attending surveyor as each space is completed. Typical scopes:
list: Third renewal survey gauging on a Supramax bulk carrier in the Chalkis Shipyards dock: hold frames, hopper and topside tanks, hatch coamings and transverse sections.
Pre-docking gauging of a Handysize bulk carrier at anchor in the South Euboean Gulf, so plate can be ordered before the ship enters the yard.
Wall-thickness checks on scrubber wash-water and overboard lines on a general cargo ship during an afloat retrofit at the yard quays.
Docking-survey gauging of a ro-pax ferry's bottom shell, sea chests and stern area during its winter dry-docking.
Magnetic particle crack detection at hatch corners and lower hopper knuckles on an older bulk carrier, alongside the hold gauging for its survey.

logistics: Athens International Airport is the arrival point, and Chalkida is reached by motorway north through Attica and Boeotia, crossing to Evia by the high-level bridge. Passes for Chalkis Shipyards and for the cargo quays are applied for through the ship's agent with technician certificates and equipment lists; launches for ships at anchor are booked the same way. As Greece is a Schengen state, technicians need Schengen visas issued in India, and we recommend confirming the job when the yard fixes the docking slot, because the visa process sets the earliest date the team can arrive.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a ship while it waits for the Euripus bridge to open?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A ship waiting at anchor for a passage slot may be there for hours or overnight, which is enough for deck plating, hatch covers and coamings, and perhaps a ballast tank the crew has already prepared. Launch transfers are arranged through the agent. Because the passage time is set by the current and the bridge opening, we plan to finish the most important readings early.

faqs.q: How large a ship can dock at Chalkida?
faqs.a: Chalkis Shipyards dry-docks ships up to around Supramax size, which covers most Handysize and Supramax bulk carriers, mid-size tankers, general cargo ships and ferries. Larger ships are usually docked at the Elefsina bay or Perama yards near Piraeus. The yard has announced plans for a bigger floating dock, so confirm the current limits with the yard when choosing where to dock.

faqs.q: Can gauging at Chalkida include the ballast water treatment system pipework?
faqs.a: Yes. Ballast water and scrubber pipework fitted in recent retrofits can be measured with the same ultrasonic gauges used on the hull, and we report it in piping tables with isometric sketches. Pipe runs inside ballast tanks and overboard sections near the shell are usually the first to thin, so we put them first when the system has been in service for a few years.

faqs.q: Can one trip cover a docking at Chalkida and work near Piraeus?
faqs.a: Usually. Chalkida is within road reach of Perama, Salamina and the Elefsina bay, so a team can move between yards and anchorages during one visit. Send the dates for every ship in the programme and we plan the sequence and a visa period that covers them all, leaving some margin for docking dates that slip.
